★ **Roll with resistance**: acknowledge perspective, reflect ambivalence, offer choices rather than argue

rows.label: Compare
items: Ask–provide–ask: elicit knowledge, share concise information, invite interpretation
Maintenance: reinforce gains, anticipate triggers; recurrence → revisit goals without shame

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Avoid the righting reflex**: lectures, scare tactics, unsolicited commands provoke defensiveness
Agreement with clinician is not commitment; obtain a patient-selected next step
Stage of change can vary by behavior and over time

table.title: Match counseling to readiness
rows: Raise awareness, no pressure; revisit at follow-up

motivational-interviewing.evidence: Established behavioral counseling principles; no guideline-dependent thresholds.

multiple-gestation.name: Multiple gestation
multiple-gestation.scope: Dichorionic diamniotic (lambda sign), monochorionic diamniotic (T-sign), monochorionic monoamniotic, twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), selective FGR, delivery timing recommendations
multiple-gestation.core: Chorionicity and amnionicity determine twin-specific surveillance, complications, and delivery timing; establish both on first-trimester ultrasound.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dizygotic twins: ovulation induction/assisted reproduction, maternal age, family history
Monozygotic splitting timing determines placental and sac sharing

rows.label: Clues
items: Uterus larger than dates, exaggerated pregnancy symptoms; ultrasound confirms fetal number
★ Shared placenta with **oligohydramnios/polyhydramnios sequence** → TTTS; small/absent donor bladder
Selective FGR: one small twin, discordant estimated weights; assess each umbilical artery Doppler

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental vascular anastomoses permit imbalanced flow in monochorionic twins
Donor hypovolemia reduces urine; recipient hypervolemia increases urine and cardiac strain

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **First-trimester ultrasound** identifies shared placenta and intertwin membrane
Monochorionic diamniotic → ultrasound **every 2 weeks from 16 weeks** for fluid/bladders
Serial growth in all twins; Doppler and more frequent assessment when growth discordance develops
TTTS donor deepest pocket ≤2 cm, recipient ≥8 cm; staging incorporates bladder, Doppler, hydrops

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ TTTS stages II–IV at 16–26 weeks → **fetoscopic laser ablation** of placental anastomoses
Asymptomatic stage I → at least weekly surveillance; refer fetal intervention center if progression/symptoms
★ Diamniotic twins with **first twin cephalic** may deliver vaginally with experienced team
Monoamniotic twins → cesarean; fetal deterioration, preeclampsia, or severe growth issues may require earlier delivery

rows.label: Complications
items: Preterm birth, preeclampsia, anemia, gestational diabetes, postpartum hemorrhage
Monoamniotic cord entanglement; monochorionic co-twin death can cause surviving twin neurologic injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention; optimize iron/nutrition; single-embryo transfer reduces iatrogenic multiples

rows.label: Mimics
items: Incorrect dates/macrosomia: enlarged uterus but singleton on imaging
Twin anemia-polycythemia sequence: discordant MCA velocities without major fluid imbalance

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, **Northern European ancestry**, family history; EBV, smoking, low vitamin D

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular loss, poor color vision, afferent pupillary defect, often normal fundus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired ipsilateral adduction, contralateral abducting nystagmus; convergence intact
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse/optic neuritis → **high-dose IV methylprednisolone**, not low-dose prednisone; refractory → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

myocarditis.name: Myocarditis
myocarditis.scope: Viral myocarditis, postviral heart failure, elevated cardiac biomarkers, ECG changes, cardiac MRI, supportive heart failure therapy
myocarditis.core: New chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure after a viral syndrome raises concern for inflammatory myocardial injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent viral illness, autoimmune disease, immune checkpoint inhibitors and selected drug hypersensitivity
Chagas exposure and giant-cell/eosinophilic disorders matter in selected epidemiologic or fulminant presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort, palpitations; tachycardia disproportionate to fever
Troponin elevation, nonspecific ST–T abnormalities, ventricular ectopy; normal initial studies do not exclude
★ Syncope, sustained ventricular arrhythmia, high-grade AV block or shock → **high-risk myocarditis**
Concurrent pericarditis may produce pleuritic positional pain and diffuse ST elevation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Direct injury and immune-mediated inflammation damage cardiomyocytes → edema, necrosis and ventricular dysfunction
Residual scar creates an arrhythmic substrate even when systolic function improves

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ECG, troponin, BNP and **echocardiography** assess injury, rhythm and function
★ **Cardiac MRI** identifies edema and nonischemic late gadolinium enhancement
Exclude ACS with coronary assessment when presentation/risk warrants; troponin alone cannot distinguish
Endomyocardial biopsy for selected fulminant, arrhythmic or unexplained progressive disease when etiology changes treatment
Routine broad viral serology rarely establishes myocardial cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stable systolic HF → **diuresis and guideline-directed HF drugs**; defer beta blocker during shock
Hemodynamic compromise → ICU, vasopressors/inotropes and temporary mechanical circulatory support when refractory
Treat arrhythmias/AV block; pacing or defibrillation support when necessary
No routine steroids for presumed viral disease; giant-cell, eosinophilic and immune-mediated forms may need immunosuppression
Avoid NSAIDs for isolated myocarditis with HF; pericarditic pain requires individualized assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, persistent HF, ventricular tachycardia, sudden death and intracardiac thrombosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Restrict strenuous exercise during active inflammation; return after symptom, imaging and rhythm reassessment
Classic restriction 3–6 months; newer guidance allows earlier individualized return in selected fully recovered athletes
Follow-up echo/MRI, ambulatory ECG and exercise testing guide clearance

rows.label: Mimics
items: MI: coronary distribution ischemia/scar and culprit artery
Stress cardiomyopathy: characteristic reversible wall-motion pattern
Pericarditis alone: pericardial inflammation without myocardial dysfunction

needlestick-injuries.name: Needlestick injuries and bloodborne pathogen exposure
needlestick-injuries.scope: Hepatitis B postexposure prophylaxis, HIV postexposure prophylaxis, hepatitis C monitoring, tetanus prophylaxis in puncture wounds
needlestick-injuries.core: After blood exposure, wash immediately, report promptly, assess the source and start time-sensitive prophylaxis before results if transmission risk warrants.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Deep hollow-bore injury, visibly bloody device, intravascular needle and viremic source increase transmission risk
Mucosal/nonintact skin blood contact qualifies; intact skin contact alone usually does not

rows.label: Clues
items: Often no acute symptoms; exposure history and source status determine immediate decisions
Acute fever/rash after exposure → evaluate HIV seroconversion; jaundice/transaminitis → hepatitis assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Direct inoculation bypasses epithelial barriers; early HIV replication can be interrupted before established infection
HBV vaccination establishes protective antibody; HCV lacks vaccine or proven postexposure drug prophylaxis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Source: **HIV Ag/Ab, HBsAg, HCV RNA** or anti-HCV with reflex RNA
Exposed worker baseline: HIV Ag/Ab, HBV immunity status, anti-HCV/reflex RNA; creatinine/AST/ALT for PEP
★ HIV final follow-up: **Ag/Ab + NAT at 12 weeks**; earlier testing for delayed/missed PEP
HCV follow-up if indicated: **RNA at 3–6 weeks**, anti-HCV/reflex RNA at 4–6 months

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Wash with soap/water, flush mucosa; **no squeezing, bleach or caustic antiseptics**
★ HIV PEP: start immediately, ideally hours and within **72 hours**, continue 28 days
Preferred HIV PEP: **bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide**
HIV-negative source → stop PEP unless acute infection suspected; suppressed source → individualized expert assessment
No HCV PEP; detected infection → direct-acting antiviral evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: HIV/HBV/HCV acquisition, medication adverse effects, anxiety; pregnancy does not justify delaying indicated HIV PEP

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety needles, sharps containers, no recapping; pre-exposure HBV immunization with documented response
Puncture wound: tetanus booster if last dose ≥5 years or date unknown; no prophylactic antibiotics
Primary tetanus series unknown/incomplete → vaccine + TIG
Puncture + HIV/severe immunodeficiency → TIG regardless of prior tetanus vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbloody saliva/urine: no meaningful HIV exposure unless blood contamination
Community discarded needle: low/uncertain risk; individualized assessment rather than automatic risk equivalence

neonatal-respiratory-distress.name: Neonatal respiratory distress
neonatal-respiratory-distress.scope: Transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome, meconium aspiration syndrome, persistent PH
neonatal-respiratory-distress.core: Tachypnea, retractions, grunting, or cyanosis after birth requires stabilization while gestational age, delivery history, and imaging narrow the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prematurity/maternal diabetes → RDS; cesarean without labor → TTN; post-term/meconium → aspiration
Maternal fever, prolonged membrane rupture or inadequate GBS prophylaxis raise concern for infectious pneumonia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Apnea, bradycardia, poor perfusion or severe hypoxemia** → immediate neonatal resuscitation
PPHN: labile hypoxemia, preductal right-hand saturation higher than postductal foot saturation
Unilateral absent breath sounds or abrupt deterioration → pneumothorax; scaphoid abdomen → diaphragmatic hernia
TTN improves within 24–72 hours; persistent/worsening disease warrants reassessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Poor lung expansion, airway obstruction or V/Q mismatch impairs oxygenation
PPHN: persistently high pulmonary resistance causes right-to-left ductal/atrial shunting

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry, blood gas and chest radiograph** after initial stabilization
Pre/postductal saturation comparison and echocardiography for suspected PPHN; exclude structural heart disease
Possible infection → blood culture and CBC; biomarkers cannot independently exclude sepsis
Persistent unexplained hypoxemia → echocardiography rather than assuming primary pulmonary disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Warmth, oxygen titrated to neonatal targets; **CPAP** for breathing infant with distress
Apnea/gasping or HR <100 → positive-pressure ventilation; ineffective ventilation requires corrective steps/advanced airway
RDS with increasing oxygen need → intratracheal surfactant; mechanical ventilation if noninvasive support fails
★ PPHN → lung recruitment/oxygenation, **inhaled nitric oxide** for suitable term/near-term infants; refractory → ECMO
Meconium: no routine tracheal suction; suction only obstructed ventilation; suspected sepsis → ampicillin/gentamicin

rows.label: Complications
items: Air leak, hypoxic brain injury, death; prematurity/ventilation → bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Antenatal corticosteroids when preterm delivery expected; avoid elective delivery before 39 weeks
Treat maternal infection, provide indicated intrapartum GBS prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cyanotic congenital heart disease: abnormal cardiac anatomy on echo
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: bowel in chest; intubate and decompress stomach, avoid bag-mask ventilation

table.title: Lung patterns
rows: Low volumes, diffuse ground glass/air bronchograms
May be normal or reflect trigger

neonatal-resuscitation.name: Neonatal resuscitation
neonatal-resuscitation.scope: NRP algorithm, initial steps (warm, dry, stimulate), PPV indications (apnea, HR < 100), chest compressions (HR < 60), epinephrine, target SpO2
neonatal-resuscitation.core: At birth, effective ventilation drives heart-rate recovery; escalate support according to the response after each timed intervention.

rows.label: Definition
items: Apgar: appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration, each scored 0–2 at 1 and 5 min
Score 1: acrocyanosis, pulse <100, grimace, some flexion, irregular breathing

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **Right-hand preductal pulse oximetry**; targets: 2 min 65–70%, 5 min 80–85%, 10 min 85–95%
Auscultate HR initially; ECG improves continuous measurement during advanced support
Oxygen start: ≥35 wk **21%**; 32–34 wk 21–30%; <32 wk 30–100%, titrated

rows.label: Use when
items: Vigorous term newborn → skin-to-skin, routine care; defer cord clamping ≥60 seconds
★ Poor tone/breathing → **warm, dry, position airway, stimulate**; initial assessment within first minute
Spontaneous breathing plus distress/cyanosis → oxygen titration; consider CPAP

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ Poor PPV → **reposition, reseal, open mouth, suction obstruction, raise pressure, alternate airway**
Compressions: two-thumb encircling technique, depth one-third chest; 90 compressions + 30 breaths/min
Epinephrine: **0.01–0.03 mg/kg IV/IO**; repeat every 3–5 min; umbilical venous access preferred

rows.label: Traps
items: No routine suction, including meconium; suction only suspected airway obstruction
★ **2025 PPV rate 30–60/min**; older teaching 40–60/min
Persistent bradycardia → check pneumothorax/hypovolemia; blood loss → saline or uncrossmatched blood

table.title: Timed escalation
rows: Stop compressions; continue ventilation if needed

neutropenia.name: Neutropenia
neutropenia.scope: Benign ethnic neutropenia (Duffy-null), drug-induced neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, autoimmune neutropenia, ANC thresholds, evaluation and management
neutropenia.core: Infection risk tracks the depth and duration of neutrophil depletion; fever with severe neutropenia is an antibiotic emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cytotoxic chemotherapy, marrow malignancy, viral infection, autoimmune disease, B12/folate/copper deficiency
Clozapine, methimazole, propylthiouracil, TMP–SMX and other drugs can cause agranulocytosis
Duffy-null associated neutrophil counts: stable isolated reduction without increased infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Oral ulcers, gingivitis, recurrent bacterial/fungal infections; inflammatory signs and pus may be absent
Cyclic mouth ulcers/infections suggest cyclic neutropenia; multiple cytopenias suggest marrow disease
Drug-associated fever or sore throat → urgent CBC, especially with antithyroid drugs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced marrow production, peripheral destruction or splenic sequestration lowers circulating neutrophils
Mucosal barrier injury plus impaired innate defense permits rapid invasive bacterial infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ANC = WBC × (% neutrophils + bands)/100**; repeat CBC with differential and smear
Mild: 1000–1500/µL; moderate: 500–1000; **severe <500**; profound <100
★ Febrile neutropenia: **≥38.3°C once or ≥38.0°C for ≥1 hour**, ANC <500 or expected decline
Obtain peripheral/line blood cultures, targeted cultures and imaging without delaying antibiotics
Persistent unexplained severe counts, abnormal smear or other cytopenias → marrow evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Febrile severe neutropenia → **IV cefepime**, piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem promptly
Add vancomycin for shock, suspected line/skin infection, pneumonia or documented resistant gram-positive infection
★ Stop culprit drug; G-CSF for selected severe/drug-related cases and high-risk chemotherapy settings
Carefully selected low-risk stable patients → oral ciprofloxacin + amoxicillin–clavulanate with reliable close follow-up
High-risk persistent fever 4–7 days → fungal evaluation and empiric **caspofungin**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pseudomonas sepsis, invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis, neutropenic enterocolitis; avoid rectal instrumentation
**Ecthyma gangrenosum**: bulla → painless black necrotic ulcer, Pseudomonas bacteremia; antipseudomonal drug, not steroids

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, oral care; selected prolonged profound neutropenia → antibacterial/antifungal prophylaxis
Stable Duffy-null pattern → reassurance after excluding other causes; no unnecessary G-CSF

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lymphopenia: opportunistic infection risk with preserved ANC
Acute leukemia: blasts and additional cytopenias

nonalcoholic-fatty-liver-disease.name: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
nonalcoholic-fatty-liver-disease.scope: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, steatohepatitis, fibrosis risk, lifestyle modification
nonalcoholic-fatty-liver-disease.core: Metabolic risk with hepatic steatosis requires fibrosis assessment; fibrosis stage, rather than aminotransferase level, predicts liver-related outcomes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Central obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea
Lean individuals can be affected; quantify alcohol and exclude medication-related or other hepatic causes

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic; incidental echogenic liver or mild transaminase elevation, commonly ALT >AST
Normal enzymes do not exclude advanced disease; thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly or low albumin suggest progression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin resistance increases hepatic fat delivery/synthesis; lipotoxicity promotes inflammation and stellate-cell fibrosis
MASH adds hepatocyte ballooning and inflammation; simple steatosis lacks these injury features

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **FIB-4 first** in at-risk adults; <1.3 usually low risk, ≥1.3 → elastography/ELF
Age >65: use >2.0 threshold for further assessment; FIB-4 less reliable under 35 or acutely ill
★ FIB-4 >2.67 or discordant/high-risk tests → **hepatology referral**
Ultrasound detects steatosis but misses mild disease; biopsy for uncertainty or selected staging decisions
Exclude viral hepatitis, excess alcohol, drug injury; evaluate other etiologies when clinical findings atypical

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Weight loss, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet**; sustained >10% loss often needed for fibrosis improvement
Optimize diabetes/lipids/BP; statins safe in compensated disease; selected bariatric surgery for qualifying obesity
★ Noncirrhotic MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis → specialist consideration of **resmetirom or semaglutide**
Selected biopsy-proven disease → pioglitazone, or vitamin E in nondiabetic noncirrhotic adults after risk discussion
Decompensated cirrhosis → complication management/transplant assessment; avoid treating isolated enzymes as severity marker

rows.label: Complications
items: Cirrhosis, HCC, portal hypertension; cardiovascular disease is a major competing mortality risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Metabolic risk control, minimize alcohol; repeat fibrosis assessment more often with diabetes/multiple metabolic risks
Cirrhosis → HCC and variceal surveillance; hepatitis A/B vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol-associated disease: significant alcohol exposure, often AST predominance
Autoimmune hepatitis: high IgG/autoantibodies; iron overload: elevated transferrin saturation

obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.name: Obesity and bariatric surgery
obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.scope: Lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy (GLP-1 receptor agonists), indications for bariatric surgery, postoperative nutritional and surgical complications
obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.core: Chronic excess adiposity with metabolic complications; sustained treatment combines nutrition, activity, behavioral support, medications, and sometimes metabolic surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Calorie-dense diet, inactivity, sleep deprivation, genetic susceptibility, food insecurity
Glucocorticoids, antipsychotics, insulin; investigate endocrine causes when examination suggests them

rows.label: Clues
items: BMI ≥30 kg/m²; central adiposity predicts cardiometabolic risk
Screen for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, fatty liver, osteoarthritis, depression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Adipose inflammation and insulin resistance; appetite regulation favors weight regain after weight loss
Bypass and sleeve alter gut signaling and intake; bypass additionally decreases nutrient absorption

rows.label: Dx
items: Weight trajectory, medication review, eating-disorder assessment; A1c, lipids, liver enzymes
★ Postoperative **tachycardia**, fever, abdominal pain → investigate anastomotic leak urgently

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Structured calorie deficit, activity, behavioral follow-up; **5–10% weight loss** improves metabolic disease
Child: **cut liquid calories** first (juice, excess whole milk); cause is total calorie surplus
Medications: BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with comorbidity; semaglutide or tirzepatide plus lifestyle changes
★ Avoid GLP-1 agents with **MEN 2/medullary thyroid carcinoma** history; avoid weight-loss drugs during pregnancy
★ **Surgical referral** by eligibility below; assess nutritional, operative, psychosocial readiness and lifelong follow-up

rows.label: Complications
items: Early: leak, bleeding, VTE; later: stricture, rapid-weight-loss gallstones, internal hernia with intermittent pain
Roux-en-Y: dumping after sugary meals, marginal ulcers; iron, B12, calcium, vitamin D deficiencies
Persistent vomiting → thiamine deficiency; give thiamine promptly before carbohydrate loading

rows.label: Prevention
items: Lifelong supplements and nutritional surveillance after surgery; avoid NSAIDs and tobacco after bypass
Small meals, fewer simple sugars for dumping; delay conception during rapid postoperative weight loss

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cushing syndrome: violaceous striae, proximal weakness, easy bruising
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, bradycardia; usually modest weight gain

obstructive-sleep-apnea.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
obstructive-sleep-apnea.scope: risk factors, clinical features (excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring), polysomnography, CPAP, cardiovascular complications
obstructive-sleep-apnea.core: Recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep causes intermittent hypoxemia and arousals, often presenting as loud snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, aging, retrognathia and upper-airway crowding
Alcohol/sedatives worsen collapse; children often have adenotonsillar hypertrophy; risk rises after menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed apneas, gasping/choking, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia
Resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, secondary polycythemia or recurrent drowsy-driving episodes raise suspicion
Children may show hyperactivity, learning problems, enuresis or poor growth rather than sleepiness
Normal awake oxygen saturation does not exclude severe nocturnal disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sleep-related reduction in pharyngeal tone collapses vulnerable airway despite persistent respiratory effort
Intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic surges drive hypertension; fragmentation impairs attention and vigilance
Sleep-related hypoventilation with nocturnal hypercapnia → morning headaches

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Polysomnography** confirms; screening tools such as STOP-BANG estimate risk, not diagnosis
Uncomplicated high-risk adults → home sleep apnea test acceptable; negative/inconclusive → in-laboratory study
★ AHI **≥5/hour with symptoms/comorbidity**, or ≥15 regardless of symptoms, establishes adult OSA
AHI 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe; pediatric thresholds differ
Cardiorespiratory disease, suspected hypoventilation, chronic opioids or neuromuscular weakness → laboratory polysomnography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CPAP** for symptomatic OSA and most moderate/severe disease; optimize mask fit/adherence
Weight loss, exercise, lateral sleep positioning; avoid bedtime alcohol and sedatives
★ CPAP-intolerant or selected mild/moderate disease → **mandibular advancement device**
Child adenotonsillar hypertrophy → adenotonsillectomy, even with pulmonary hypertension; selected adults → surgery, hypoglossal stimulation
Counsel sleepy patients to avoid driving until controlled; do not rely on stimulants before treating obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Systemic hypertension, arrhythmias, stroke risk, pulmonary hypertension in selected patients
Motor vehicle/work accidents, impaired cognition, mood disturbance
Awake postoperative hypercapnia → **CPAP/BiPAP**; reintubate only if obtunded or failing noninvasive support

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight, reassess after major weight change; continue PAP around surgery with monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Central apnea: absent respiratory effort during pauses
Narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleep-onset REM features
OHS: persistent daytime hypercapnia

opioid-prescribing-and-safety.name: Opioid prescribing and safety
opioid-prescribing-and-safety.scope: Chronic opioid therapy, prescription drug monitoring, opioid tapering, misuse risk assessment, managing refill requests, naloxone co-prescribing
opioid-prescribing-and-safety.core: Use opioids only when expected functional benefit exceeds harm, with shared goals, ongoing reassessment, and a plan for safer prescribing.

rows.label: Principle
items: Chronic pain: prefer nonopioid options; individualize benefit–harm assessment without rigid dose ceilings
CDC outpatient guideline excludes sickle-cell pain, cancer treatment, palliative and end-of-life care

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Before starting: **PDMP, substance-use/mental-health review**, functional goals, risk discussion
Immediate-release, lowest effective dose; reassess at 1–4 weeks after starting/escalating, then regularly
★ **Offer naloxone**: overdose risk with prior overdose, OUD, apnea, benzodiazepines, higher doses

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid opioid–benzodiazepine combinations when possible; discuss alcohol and driving impairment
Never dismiss/prescribe solely from risk score, urine result, or early refill request

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Refill concern → **nonjudgmental review**, PDMP, call prescriber; assess withdrawal, pain, misuse
Harms exceed benefits → collaborative taper; imminent overdose danger → urgent intervention
Opioid-use disorder → offer buprenorphine/methadone; continue pain care and arrange treatment support

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **No abrupt forced discontinuation**; individualized taper may take months/years
Toxicology testing supports safety, not punishment; confirm unexpected findings and assay limitations
Physical dependence/tolerance alone during supervised treatment does not establish opioid-use disorder

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.scope: Clinical diagnosis (Heberden/Bouchard nodes, activity-related pain), radiographic findings, nonpharmacologic therapy, oral and topical NSAIDs, injections
osteoarthritis.core: Activity-related joint pain with brief morning stiffness, crepitus and bony enlargement suggests degenerative joint disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, **obesity** (strongest modifiable), prior trauma, malalignment, repetitive occupational loading
Family history, particularly hand disease; obesity affects both mechanical and metabolic risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning stiffness generally **<30 minutes**; pain improves with rest early in disease
Knees, hips, first carpometacarpal, DIP and PIP commonly involved; MCP usually spared
Heberden nodes: DIP; Bouchard nodes: PIP; reduced motion and varus/valgus deformity
Hip disease: groin pain with restricted internal rotation; referred pain can localize to knee

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Articular cartilage loss, subchondral remodeling and osteophytes; low-grade synovial inflammation
Joint pain arises from innervated surrounding structures rather than aneural cartilage itself

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical presentation → **clinical diagnosis**; imaging unnecessary for straightforward mild disease
Weight-bearing radiographs if uncertain, severe or worsening: asymmetric joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts
★ Hot acutely swollen joint → **arthrocentesis**; not an OA flare; mild cool effusion → x-ray, simple analgesic
OA fluid noninflammatory: usually WBC <2000/µL; inflammatory markers generally normal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **exercise, strengthening, weight loss**; cane contralateral to painful hip/knee
★ Knee/hand pain → **topical diclofenac**; oral NSAID if insufficient and renal/GI/CV risks acceptable
Acetaminophen if unable to use NSAIDs (older exam questions may expect it first); duloxetine for persistent pain
Intra-articular glucocorticoid for short-term relief; avoid routine opioids and hyaluronic acid injections
Severe pain/function loss despite conservative treatment → **joint replacement**

rows.label: Complications
items: Functional limitation, falls, reduced activity and secondary deconditioning
NSAIDs → GI bleeding, AKI, fluid retention; arthroplasty → infection or VTE

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Weight loss** best prevents knee OA, beyond exercise alone; conditioning, injury prevention; no complete joint rest

rows.label: Mimics
items: Rheumatoid arthritis: prolonged stiffness, boggy symmetric MCP/wrist synovitis, marginal erosions, DIP spared
CPPD: acute inflammatory flares, chondrocalcinosis
Septic arthritis: fever, severe painful passive motion, positive synovial culture
Trochanteric bursitis: lateral hip pain over greater trochanter, not groin pain

osteoarthritis.evidence: Not checked online; established ACR/Arthritis Foundation principles.

osteonecrosis.name: Osteonecrosis
osteonecrosis.scope: Avascular necrosis of femoral head, risk factors (corticosteroids, alcohol, sickle cell, trauma), MRI sensitivity, crescent sign on plain radiograph, core decompression, joint replacement
osteonecrosis.core: Progressive deep hip or groin pain after steroid exposure, heavy alcohol use, sickle cell disease, or trauma suggests femoral-head ischemia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Glucocorticoids**, excessive alcohol, sickle cell vaso-occlusion, femoral neck fracture or hip dislocation
SLE, transplantation, decompression exposure; bilateral disease common with systemic causes

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight-bearing pain progressing to rest/night pain; limited internal rotation and abduction
Antalgic gait, referred thigh/knee pain; early examination can be nearly normal
Sudden worsening suggests subchondral fracture or articular collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Interrupted subchondral blood supply → osteocyte death, microfractures, eventual joint surface collapse
Repair cannot keep pace with mechanical loading; secondary degenerative arthritis follows

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs** first; early disease may be radiographically occult
★ Persistent suspicion despite normal films → **MRI**, most sensitive early test
Later films: patchy sclerosis/lucency; crescent sign indicates subchondral fracture, then flattening
Evaluate contralateral hip when symptoms or systemic risk suggest bilateral involvement

rows.label: Tx
items: Protected weight-bearing, cane/crutches, NSAIDs, orthopedic referral; analgesics do not restore perfusion
★ Before collapse → **core decompression** in selected symptomatic lesions; joint-preserving options depend on extent
Advanced collapse or secondary arthritis → total hip arthroplasty
Reduce avoidable steroid/alcohol exposure; manage sickle cell and other underlying disorders

rows.label: Complications
items: Femoral-head collapse, painful osteoarthritis, loss of mobility and function
Arthroplasty: infection, dislocation, loosening; younger patients may require revision

rows.label: Prevention
items: Use lowest effective glucocorticoid exposure; counsel against heavy alcohol consumption
Prompt reduction of traumatic hip dislocation limits ischemic time; monitor high-risk post-traumatic hips
Activity modification during evaluation reduces loading on vulnerable subchondral bone

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hip osteoarthritis: gradual activity pain, joint-space narrowing and osteophytes rather than early isolated necrosis
Septic arthritis: fever, severe pain with passive motion; urgent aspiration
Femoral neck stress fracture: overuse, fracture line or marrow edema on MRI
Osteomyelitis: fever, elevated ESR/CRP; osteonecrosis markers usually normal

osteonecrosis.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic diagnosis and stage-based treatment.

osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.scope: DEXA scan T-score criteria, screening guidelines, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, vertebral compression fractures, bisphosphonates
osteoporosis.core: Fragility fracture or markedly reduced bone density identifies skeletal weakness, often silent until hip or vertebral fracture.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Postmenopause, older age, White/Asian ancestry, BMI <20, parental fragility hip fracture, smoking, alcohol >2 drinks/day
Glucocorticoids, early or surgical menopause, hypogonadism, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, immobility, rheumatoid arthritis

rows.label: Clues
items: Height loss, kyphosis, acute back pain with **midline point tenderness** after trivial strain suggest vertebral compression
Neurologic deficits, fever, or nocturnal pain suggest alternative spinal pathology

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bone resorption exceeds formation; microarchitecture deteriorates despite normally mineralized remaining bone
Estrogen deficiency increases osteoclast activity; steroids suppress osteoblasts and reduce calcium balance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Hip/spine DXA**; use T-scores in postmenopausal women and men ≥50
★ Hip/vertebral low-trauma fracture establishes diagnosis regardless of DXA; acute vertebral pain → **spine x-ray** before DXA
CBC, calcium, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D; targeted secondary-cause testing
Younger adults: Z-score ≤−2 suggests below-age bone density; T-score alone insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Alendronate or zoledronic acid** for qualifying fracture, osteoporosis-range DXA, or high FRAX risk; raloxifene/estrogen contraindicated after VTE
Osteopenia: treat if 10-year hip risk ≥3% or major osteoporotic risk ≥20%
Oral bisphosphonate: fasting water, remain upright; avoid esophageal disease, hypocalcemia, severe kidney dysfunction
Very high risk → teriparatide/romosozumab then antiresorptive; stopping denosumab requires follow-on antiresorptive
Vertebral pain: analgesia, mobilization, short bracing; procedures reserved for selected refractory cases

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Hip fracture** → immobility, thromboembolism, excess mortality
Bisphosphonates: rare jaw osteonecrosis/atypical femur fracture; denosumab: hypocalcemia, rebound vertebral fractures

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen **women ≥65**, younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; evidence insufficient for routine male screening
**Smoking cessation**, less heavy alcohol outrank supplements; weight-bearing/resistance exercise, fall prevention, dietary calcium/vitamin D
Prednisone-equivalent ≥2.5 mg/day for >3 months → fracture-risk assessment; prevent with **alendronate**, not estrogen/raloxifene

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomalacia: defective mineralization, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase
Myeloma: anemia, renal injury, lytic lesions; metastatic fracture: destructive focal lesion

osteoporosis.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2025](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/osteoporosis-screening%20); treatment: established fracture-risk framework.

palliative-and-hospice-care.name: Palliative and hospice care
palliative-and-hospice-care.scope: Hospice eligibility, pain control, goals of care, surrogate requests
palliative-and-hospice-care.core: Palliative care relieves suffering at any illness stage; hospice centers care on comfort when prognosis and patient goals support a terminal-care benefit.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Patient goals and informed consent** guide intervention burdens; symptom relief remains an obligation
Proportionate opioids for pain/dyspnea permissible despite risks; reassess sedation/respiration
Codeine fails → morphine/oxycodone; pain mimics depression; wears off early → shorten interval

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Ask understanding/values → discuss prognosis → recommend a goal-concordant plan
Assess capacity; use advance directive, then authorized surrogate: substituted judgment/best interests
★ Titrate **opioids**, short-acting for breakthrough; constipation → keep dose, add stimulant laxative

rows.label: Don't
items: DNR ≠ no antibiotics, fluids, nutrition or other desired treatment
Capable patient’s informed wishes override surrogate requests
No nonbeneficial interventions; explain reasoning, offer alternatives, seek ethics review for conflict

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Refractory terminal suffering → proportional palliative sedation, specialist review and consent
Emergency, unknown preferences → stabilize while clarifying wishes; honor documented refusals
Advanced dementia refusing intake → comfort hand-feeding by mouth; no tubes or IV

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Hospice: **≤6-month prognosis** if usual course; longer survival permits recertification
Hospice: unrelated conditions remain treatable; no DNR requirement; enrollment revocable if goals change
Cancer pain: escalating requests → tolerance/progression, not addiction; past OUD never limits analgesia

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

table.title: Care settings
rows: Adjust with hospice team; avoid readmission

parasitic-infections.name: Parasitic infections
parasitic-infections.scope: Strongyloidiasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, cryptosporidiosis, ascariasis, schistosomiasis, pinworm (enterobiasis), cysticercosis, eosinophilia workup, antiparasitic therapy
parasitic-infections.core: Exposure, organ pattern, and immune status identify the parasite; eosinophilia favors tissue-invasive helminths rather than intestinal protozoa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Contaminated food/water, endemic travel, freshwater contact, barefoot soil exposure, household crowding
Steroids/HTLV-1 predispose to Strongyloides hyperinfection; advanced HIV predisposes to persistent cryptosporidiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Ascariasis: transient cough/eosinophilic infiltrates during larval migration; later intestinal or biliary obstruction
Pinworm: nocturnal perianal/vulvar itch, dysuria with normal UA; household clustering
Cysticercosis: seizures or hydrocephalus; ingestion of **T. solium eggs**, not pork cysts
Cutaneous larva migrans: soil contact; pruritic **serpiginous tracks**; animal hookworm larvae → albendazole or ivermectin

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Giardia blunts microvilli → **fat/carbohydrate malabsorption**; invasive protozoa can affect liver, urinary tract, or CNS
Strongyloides autoinfection permits lifelong persistence and dissemination after immunosuppression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unexplained **eosinophilia** → travel/drug history, serial stool O&P, targeted Strongyloides serology
★ Steroids + eosinophilia or infiltrates → **Strongyloides hyperinfection**: **duodenal aspirate** larvae; stool O&P often misses
Diarrhea → stool antigen/PCR for protozoa; single routine O&P can miss infection
★ Pinworm → **morning tape test** before washing; stool testing insensitive
Brain MRI/CT for cysticercosis; eye examination before antiparasitics; assess lesion viability and location

rows.label: Tx
items: Rehydrate; ascariasis → albendazole; bowel obstruction → surgical evaluation before deworming
Pinworm → albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel; repeat after **2 weeks**, treat household simultaneously
★ Viable parenchymal cysticercosis → albendazole ± praziquantel with corticosteroids; seizures → levetiracetam
Calcified brain lesions → no antiparasitic; hydrocephalus → neurosurgical control before cysticidal treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Strongyloides hyperinfection → gram-negative sepsis, respiratory failure; eosinophilia may disappear
Amebic liver abscess; schistosomiasis → portal hypertension or bladder squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen/treat Strongyloides before **immunosuppression** after endemic exposure
Safe water, sanitation, handwashing, footwear; avoid endemic freshwater and untreated swimming water
Neurocysticercosis household contacts → **stool O&P** to find egg-shedding T. solium tapeworm carrier

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea after infection excluded
Drug hypersensitivity: eosinophilia linked to new medication, rash or organ injury

table.title: Exposure → diagnosis and treatment
rows: Camping; greasy stool, bloating; stool antigen
Dysentery, flask-shaped ulcers; stool PCR; abscess → serology
Soil; larva currens, larvae in stool
Ivermectin; hyperinfection requires prolonged daily treatment
Freshwater; hematuria (haematobium), portal fibrosis (mansoni/japonicum); eggs, serology
Confirmed E. histolytica without invasive disease

pediatric-exanthems.name: Pediatric exanthems
pediatric-exanthems.scope: Measles (rubeola), rubella (German measles), roseola infantum (HHV-6), erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19 fifth disease), scarlet fever, varicella, clinical appearance, complications
pediatric-exanthems.core: Fever with a childhood rash: use fever timing, rash progression, mucosal findings, immunization status, and pregnancy exposure to distinguish causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incomplete immunization, daycare/school exposure, travel; immunosuppression increases severe viral disease
Pregnant contacts require prompt assessment after rubella, parvovirus, or varicella exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Toxic appearance**, petechiae/purpura, hypotension, meningismus → evaluate invasive infection immediately
Measles: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis precede rash; rubella: posterior auricular/suboccipital adenopathy
Varicella: trunk/scalp predominance; oral mucosal lesions may accompany the skin eruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Parvovirus suppresses erythroid precursors; congenital infection can cause severe fetal anemia
VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia; HHV-6 commonly causes febrile illness in infants

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected measles → **airborne isolation**, notify public health; respiratory PCR plus serum IgM
Scarlet fever → rapid GAS test; negative pediatric test → throat culture
Typical roseola/fifth disease: clinical; atypical vesicles → VZV PCR; rubella → public-health serology/PCR

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scarlet fever → **penicillin or amoxicillin**; other uncomplicated exanthems generally supportive
Measles → hydration, complication care, clinician-supervised vitamin A for children
Severe/immunocompromised varicella → **IV acyclovir**; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Measles: pneumonia, encephalitis, delayed SSPE; rubella: congenital cataracts, deafness, PDA
Parvovirus: aplastic crisis, hydrops, adult symmetric polyarthritis → NSAIDs, not steroids; roseola: febrile seizures
Varicella: bacterial superinfection, pneumonia, cerebellitis; GAS: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **MMR and varicella vaccines**; live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy and severe immunosuppression
Measles exposure: MMR within 72 hours or immune globulin within 6 days for eligible contacts

rows.label: Mimics
items: Kawasaki disease: ≥5 days fever, conjunctivitis, oral/extremity changes
Drug eruption: medication exposure without characteristic infectious sequence

table.title: Signature rash
rows: Koplik spots; face → downward confluent rash
Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines, strawberry tongue

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent, traumatic, malignant, or recurrent effusion → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure
Early post-cardiac-surgery tamponade → **urgent mediastinal re-exploration**

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

perioperative-care.name: Perioperative care
perioperative-care.scope: Preoperative cardiac risk, pulmonary evaluation, surgical antibiotic prophylaxis, medication management, pain control
perioperative-care.core: Optimize active disease, estimate procedural and patient risk, and order testing only when the result could change perioperative management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **MI within 60 days**, decompensated HF → highest perioperative cardiac risk; older exam questions may expect MI within 6 months
Emergency, vascular or intrathoracic surgery; ischemic heart disease, heart failure, CKD, diabetes
Smoking, COPD, OSA, frailty, malnutrition and prior anesthesia complications

rows.label: Clues
items: Chest pain, new dyspnea, syncope or decompensated fluid overload require targeted evaluation
Poor functional capacity: inability to climb stairs or perform activities around 4 METs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Surgical stress raises myocardial oxygen demand; anesthesia can lower perfusion pressure
Sedation, pain and recumbency reduce ventilation and promote atelectasis and venous stasis
Surgical stress, pain, opioids → nonosmotic **ADH** release → transient oliguria with normal renal function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RCRI/NSQIP** plus functional assessment; no routine stress test for low-risk surgery
Elevated risk, poor/unknown capacity → stress test if management changes; cannot exercise → **pharmacologic stress imaging**
ECG for cardiovascular symptoms; echo for new/worsening HF or suspected significant valve disease
No routine chest radiograph/spirometry without respiratory findings; assess airway and OSA history
Lung resection: **predicted postoperative FEV1** best predictor of complications; predicted postoperative FEV1 <30–40% → high risk, exercise testing before deciding

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Active ACS, decompensated HF or unstable arrhythmia → defer elective surgery and stabilize
★ Continue chronic **beta blockers/statins**; do not start beta blockade on surgery day
Hold **SGLT2 inhibitors 3–4 days**; individualize GLP-1 drugs by aspiration risk; continue reduced basal insulin
★ **Cefazolin within 60 minutes** before incision; MRSA or severe beta-lactam allergy → vancomycin within 120 minutes
Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen, regional block, selective NSAID; add opioid by severity, respiratory monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial injury, AKI, delirium, pneumonia, VTE and surgical-site infection
Opioids aggravate OSA; excessive fluids can worsen pulmonary edema
New postoperative dyspnea, ↓basal breath sounds → chest radiograph first, before PE imaging or heparin

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, lung expansion exercises, early mobilization, mechanical/pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis
Anticoagulation interruption individualized; bridging reserved for highest thrombotic risk
Chronic steroid exposure with adrenal suppression → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage
Usable gut → **enteral feeding**, including distal jejunostomy, over TPN

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anxiety-related dyspnea: normal cardiopulmonary evaluation
Stable chronic disease: baseline symptoms alone do not mandate cancellation

table.title: Postoperative pain
rows: Severe pain after major abdominal surgery

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings
Abrupt onset + AF, even with prior claudication → **embolus**, not in situ thrombosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle
Subclavian stenosis proximal to vertebral origin → arm exercise reverses ipsilateral vertebral flow; brachiocephalic lesion: right arm + carotid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; acute ischemia: bedside Doppler, **arteriography with runoff**
Subclavian steal → **compare BP in both arms** (gap >15 mm Hg); confirm with duplex or **MR angiography**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia with distal target → **surgical bypass** before amputation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin, vascular consultation** without awaiting imaging; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible or nonfunctional limb (nonambulatory, contractures) → primary amputation
Popliteal aneurysm: pulsatile popliteal mass, distal emboli; large → **tibial nerve compression** (posterior knee/calf pain)

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings
Thoracic outlet syndrome: symptoms on arm abduction, no posterior-circulation ischemia

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals
Calf claudication; normal femoral, weak pedal pulses
Arm-exercise dizziness/syncope or claudication; weak ipsilateral pulse

pharyngitis.name: Pharyngitis
pharyngitis.scope: Centor score, Group A Streptococcus, rapid antigen detection, throat culture, viral pharyngitis, penicillin, peritonsillar abscess
pharyngitis.core: Most sore throats are viral; identify patients needing group A streptococcal testing and recognize deep-space infection or airway danger.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: School-age children, close contacts, crowded settings, winter/spring; GAS uncommon below age 3
Smoking, immunosuppression, incomplete vaccination broaden infectious differential

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctivitis, oral ulcers** favor viral cause; avoid unnecessary GAS testing
Centor: fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough; 1 point each
McIsaac modifies by age; score 0–1 → no test, no antibiotic; scoring never proves bacterial infection
★ **Trismus, muffled voice, unilateral bulge, uvular deviation** → peritonsillar abscess

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GAS pharyngeal infection can trigger immune-mediated rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis
Tonsillitis → peritonsillar pus: **GAS** commonest, often mixed anaerobes; deeper spread threatens airway, vessels

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No clear viral syndrome and elevated clinical score → **rapid antigen test or NAAT**
Negative rapid antigen in symptomatic child ≥3 → throat culture; adults usually need no backup
Positive test with compatible illness → treat; asymptomatic carriage generally needs no eradication
Abscess usually clinical; ultrasound/contrast neck CT if uncertain or deep-space extension suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Confirmed GAS → **penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days**; IM benzathine penicillin if adherence uncertain
Penicillin allergy: cephalexin if nonimmediate; azithromycin/clindamycin if immediate, accounting for local resistance
Viral illness → fluids, warm saline gargle, acetaminophen/ibuprofen; no antibiotics
★ Peritonsillar abscess → **drainage + amoxicillin-clavulanate**; airway assessment, IV ampicillin-sulbactam if severe

rows.label: Complications
items: Rheumatic fever prevented by timely GAS antibiotics; poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis not reliably prevented
Retropharyngeal spread, airway obstruction; Fusobacterium → internal jugular thrombophlebitis/Lemierre syndrome

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene; remain home until afebrile and ≥12–24 hours after effective GAS antibiotics
Do not routinely test asymptomatic household contacts or obtain test-of-cure

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV: posterior nodes, splenomegaly, amoxicillin-associated rash
Epiglottitis: drooling, tripod posture, stridor; avoid provocative throat examination
Diphtheria: adherent gray membrane, incomplete vaccination

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure
**Comprehensive, contextual care**: whole-person, longitudinal; tailored to culture, family, goals

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

table.title: Difficult conversations
rows: Pause; allow feelings; schedule prompt follow-up
Voice openly in patient's presence; no covert action
Capable patient hides news from family
Encourage support; respect privacy; never lie to family
Child asks prognosis, parents forbid disclosure
Explore understanding; encourage talking with parents; never lie
Negotiate adherence contract; punitive control backfires
Fluent bilingual staff acceptable; never a child

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

physiologic-changes-of-aging.name: Physiologic changes of aging
physiologic-changes-of-aging.scope: Neurologic changes, sensory changes (presbyopia, presbycusis), sleep architecture changes (early wake, reduced total sleep), cardiovascular stiffening, renal decline, pulmonary compliance
physiologic-changes-of-aging.core: Normal aging reduces organ reserve; preserved everyday independence distinguishes expected slowing from disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: Gradual changes across systems; marked disability requires evaluation rather than attribution to age
Presbyopia: reduced accommodation; presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ Slower processing and recall; **orientation and learned knowledge preserved**
★ Less slow-wave, more awakenings, earlier timing, less total sleep → **reassure**, no hypnotics
★ Isolated **↓ankle reflexes**, ↓toe vibration, impaired tandem, full strength → normal; no workup

rows.label: Use when
items: Reduced baroreflexes and maximal heart rate → orthostatic susceptibility, reduced exercise capacity
Lower renal clearance → adjust renally eliminated drugs despite normal-looking creatinine
Decreased vital capacity and cough reserve → greater respiratory illness vulnerability

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ **Arterial stiffness** → widened pulse pressure; ventricular relaxation slows
Reduced lung elastic recoil → increased lung compliance; chest wall compliance decreases
Declining concentration/dilution → fluid imbalance; reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Delirium, dementia, falls, incontinence** require evaluation; never inevitable normal aging
Depression or sedatives can explain daytime sleepiness; severe insomnia needs investigation
Unilateral hearing loss, focal weakness, **rotatory nystagmus**, rapid memory loss → disease workup

physiologic-changes-of-aging.evidence: Not checked online; established geriatric physiology.

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.name: Population health and quality improvement
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.scope: Program evaluation, outcome and process measures, health equity, PDSA cycles
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.core: Improve care for a defined population through measurable aims, iterative system changes, and attention to unequal access and outcomes.

rows.label: Principle
items: Population denominator includes eligible people missing visits, not only those receiving care
Equity: stratify outcomes by language, race/ethnicity, geography, disability, insurance, deprivation
Greater relative **primary care investment** improves population health, reduces disparities

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Define **measurable aim**, population, baseline, timeframe; engage patients/frontline staff
★ **PDSA**: plan small change → do → study results → act/adapt before scaling
Stratify measures, address interpreter/transport/cost barriers, monitor unintended consequences

rows.label: Don't
items: Do not assume a favorable outcome proves causation without comparison and context
Avoid blaming individuals for failures created by unreliable workflows

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Run/control charts distinguish routine common-cause variation from special-cause signals over time
Program evaluation: reach, fidelity, effectiveness, cost, sustainability versus original goals
Education program → measure knowledge/behavior change; small cohort cannot detect morbidity/mortality

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Process success ≠ patient benefit**; assess both and choose valid denominators
★ **Risk adjustment** improves comparison; also report disparities so adjustment cannot conceal inequity
Before–after improvement may reflect secular trends, case-mix change, regression to mean

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.evidence: Established quality-improvement and program-evaluation principles; no guideline-dependent thresholds.

postpartum-care.name: Postpartum care
postpartum-care.scope: Normal puerperal changes, lochia, uterine involution, perineal and cesarean wound healing, breastfeeding, postpartum depression screening, routine postpartum visit
postpartum-care.core: Postpartum care is an ongoing assessment of recovery, mood, infant feeding, contraception, and chronic disease after every birth.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ All postpartum patients; assess support, sleep, safety, sexual health, and reproductive goals

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Contact within **3 weeks**; comprehensive visit by **12 weeks**, with earlier risk-based review
Hypertensive disorder → BP within 7–10 days; severe hypertension → within 72 hours

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Edinburgh or PHQ-9 depression screen; assess suicidality directly after positive self-harm response
BP, bleeding, fundal tenderness; inspect perineum/incision for erythema, drainage, separation
Observe latch/milk transfer; frequent feeds, lactation support; cracked nipples → correct positioning

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Heavy bleeding (pad soaked <1 hour), fever, dyspnea, severe headache → urgent evaluation
Mood screen positive → diagnostic interview, psychotherapy/SSRI; psychosis → emergency hospitalization
Increasing wound pain/purulence → evaluate infection; breast fluctuance → ultrasound for abscess

rows.label: Traps
items: Ovulation may precede first period; discuss contraception before discharge
Lactational contraception: amenorrhea, exclusive frequent breastfeeding, infant <6 months
Postpartum hypertension and cardiomyopathy can first appear after discharge

table.title: Expected recovery
rows: Red rubra → pink serosa → white/yellow alba
Descends daily; near prepregnancy size by 6 weeks
Pain improves; pulling normal if intact; keep clean
Early cramping and fluid loss; breastfeeding intensifies cramping

postpartum-care.evidence: Visit timing checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG postpartum care](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2018/05/optimizing-postpartum-care); normal physiology established teaching.

potassium-disorders.name: Potassium disorders
potassium-disorders.scope: Hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, cardiac membrane stabilization, shift therapy, elimination
potassium-disorders.core: Potassium abnormalities can cause weakness and fatal arrhythmias; stabilize cardiac risk while identifying the cause and correcting total-body balance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hyperkalemia: AKI/CKD, RAAS blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics, tissue lysis, insulin deficiency
Hypokalemia: GI losses, loop/thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, insulin/beta-agonists, magnesium depletion

rows.label: Clues
items: Flaccid weakness, paralysis, palpitations; symptoms may be absent despite dangerous levels
★ **K ≥6.5 mmol/L, ECG changes, or rapid rise** → emergency; normal ECG not reassuring
Bradycardia/high-degree AV block with renal failure → suspect hyperkalemia; calcium before pacemaker

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extracellular K changes alter membrane excitability and cardiac conduction
Acidosis/insulin deficiency shift K outward; intracellular shifts can coexist with severe total-body depletion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG + repeat potassium**, creatinine, glucose, bicarbonate, magnesium; assess drugs and acid-base status
Hemolysis, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis → pseudohyperkalemia; repeat atraumatic draw if clinically compatible
Hypokalemia: urine K distinguishes renal wasting from extrarenal loss; interpret with BP/acid-base pattern
Do not delay treatment for confirmatory blood draw when malignant ECG changes present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Hyperkalemic ECG changes or dialysis-patient arrest → **IV calcium gluconate/chloride first**; protects myocardium only
★ Shift K inward: **IV insulin + dextrose**, nebulized albuterol; bicarbonate mainly with significant acidosis
Remove K: loop diuretic if urine output, selected binders; urgent dialysis for severe refractory/renal-failure cases
Mild/stable hypokalemia → oral KCl; <2.5, arrhythmia, paralysis, or no oral access → monitored IV replacement
★ **Correct magnesium deficiency** for refractory low K; never give IV potassium push; monitor glucose after insulin

rows.label: Complications
items: Ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, respiratory muscle failure
Overcorrection, rebound dyskalemia; insulin-induced hypoglycemia; IV potassium extravasation/phlebitis
Diuretic hypokalemia → **digoxin toxicity**, multifocal PVCs; check K first

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review supplements/salt substitutes; monitor K/creatinine after diuretic or RAAS-drug changes
Treat diarrhea/vomiting and underlying mineralocorticoid disorders; replace ongoing losses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexic weakness without explanatory electrolyte pattern
Periodic paralysis: episodic shifts, sometimes thyrotoxicosis; avoid excessive replacement causing rebound

table.title: ECG patterns
rows: Peaked T → PR prolongation → wide QRS/sine-wave
Flat T, ST depression, prominent U waves

potassium-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established electrolyte emergency principles.

psoriasis.name: Psoriasis
psoriasis.scope: Plaque psoriasis, nail pitting and onycholysis, Auspitz sign, Koebner phenomenon, psoriatic arthritis, topical and systemic therapy
psoriasis.core: Sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, usually on extensor surfaces or scalp; inspect nails and screen for inflammatory arthritis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, obesity, smoking, alcohol; stress, trauma, streptococcal infection
Lithium, beta blockers, antimalarials; systemic glucocorticoid withdrawal can trigger severe rebound

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Nail pitting, onycholysis**, oil-drop discoloration support diagnosis
Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding after scale removal; Koebner phenomenon: lesions at trauma sites
Psoriatic arthritis: morning stiffness, DIP disease, dactylitis, enthesitis, asymmetric or axial involvement
Generalized pustules, erythroderma, fever, hemodynamic disturbance → urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated TNF/IL-23/Th17 activation → accelerated keratinocyte turnover

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; biopsy if atypical; assess body surface area and functional impact
KOH scraping if fungal infection possible; inflammatory joint symptoms warrant rheumatology assessment
Before biologics: TB, hepatitis screening; before methotrexate: CBC, liver and renal tests, pregnancy assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized plaques → **topical corticosteroid + calcipotriene**; choose potency by site
Face/folds: low-potency steroid briefly or tacrolimus; emollients and scale removal aid penetration
★ Extensive/refractory disease → **narrowband UVB**, methotrexate, or targeted biologic; arthritis requires systemic control
Methotrexate contraindicated in pregnancy and significant liver disease; cyclosporine useful for rapid short-term control
Avoid routine systemic steroids; unstable erythrodermic/pustular disease → hospital support and specialist treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Joint destruction, depression, cardiometabolic disease; severe skin failure → fluid loss and infection
Systemic immunosuppression → infections; methotrexate → hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, weight management, limit alcohol; screen BP, lipids, diabetes, depression; reduce skin trauma

rows.label: Mimics
items: Tinea corporis: annular advancing edge, positive KOH
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy scale in sebaceous areas
Atopic dermatitis: flexural eczema with marked pruritus

psoriasis.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatology and psoriatic arthritis teaching.

research-ethics.name: Research ethics
research-ethics.scope: Institutional review board (IRB), vulnerable populations (prisoners, children), coercion and undue inducement, clinical equipoise, informed consent in research
research-ethics.core: Scientifically valid research requires independent oversight, fair selection, favorable risk-benefit balance, and voluntary informed participation with additional safeguards for vulnerability.

rows.label: Principle
items: Respect for persons, beneficence, justice: autonomy, minimize harm, equitable recruitment
★ **Clinical equipoise**: expert uncertainty about superior treatment; personal doubt insufficient
Vulnerability warrants safeguards, not automatic exclusion from scientifically justified studies

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **IRB approval before recruitment**; disclose conflicts, monitor harms, report unexpected problems
Explain purpose, randomization, risks, uncertain benefits, alternatives, privacy, injury care, contacts
★ **Ongoing consent**: check understanding, answer questions, update risks; withdrawal without penalty

rows.label: Don't
items: Coercion: threaten lost care, employment, grades, liberty for refusal; parole offer to prisoners
Undue influence: incentives distort voluntary judgment; reasonable reimbursement/payment permitted
Placebo causing serious harm by withholding proven care; disguise research as personalized treatment

rows.label: Exceptions
items: IRB waiver: minimal risk, impracticable otherwise, preserved rights/welfare; later disclosure when needed
Identifiable-data waiver: study also impracticable without identifiers
Emergency research: prior regulatory safeguards/approval; treatment emergency exception insufficient

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **IRB approval never replaces informed consent** unless an authorized waiver applies
Capable child's dissent generally respected despite parental permission
Therapeutic misconception: participant assumes every study decision maximizes personal clinical benefit

table.title: Additional safeguards
rows: Parental permission plus developmentally capable child's assent
Permitted research category; prisoner representative on IRB
Legally authorized representative; seek participant assent

retinal-vascular-occlusion.name: Retinal vascular occlusion
retinal-vascular-occlusion.scope: Central retinal artery occlusion (pale retina, cherry-red fovea, ocular massage), branch retinal artery occlusion, central retinal vein occlusion (blood and thunder, optic disc edema), branch retinal vein occlusion
retinal-vascular-occlusion.core: Sudden painless monocular visual loss requires urgent funduscopic localization and immediate assessment for retinal ischemia or venous obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Arterial: carotid atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, giant cell arteritis
Venous: hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma, hyperviscosity; atypical young cases warrant targeted systemic evaluation

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe asymmetric retinal ischemia → relative afferent pupillary defect
Transient monocular blackout may precede permanent arterial occlusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Arterial inflow obstruction → inner retinal infarction; venous outflow obstruction → hemorrhage and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Dilated fundus examination** urgently; OCT quantifies macular edema
★ Retinal artery occlusion → **stroke-center evaluation**, carotid imaging, ECG and cardiac source assessment
Age >50 with headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness → ESR/CRP, CBC for GCA
Fluorescein angiography assesses venous nonperfusion and neovascularization risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ CRAO → immediate emergency/stroke referral; selected early cases → **IV thrombolysis consideration**
Suspected arteritic occlusion → immediate high-dose corticosteroids; never wait for temporal artery biopsy
★ **Ocular massage/paracentesis**: historical answers; unproven, potentially harmful, not recommended by AHA
Venous occlusion with vision-limiting macular edema → intravitreal **anti-VEGF** such as aflibercept
Retinal/iris neovascularization → retinal laser; systemic anticoagulation not routine for isolated vein occlusion

rows.label: Complications
items: Arterial occlusion: permanent blindness and future ischemic stroke
Venous occlusion: recurrent macular edema, vitreous hemorrhage, neovascular glaucoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP, diabetes, lipids, smoking; arterial disease → antiplatelet/statin or anticoagulation according to embolic source
Ophthalmic surveillance after venous occlusion for delayed neovascularization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Retinal detachment: flashes, floaters, curtain-like field loss
Acute angle closure: painful red eye, halos, high IOP

table.title: Fundus pattern
rows: Sectoral retinal whitening; corresponding field defect

rh-alloimmunization.name: Rh alloimmunization
rh-alloimmunization.scope: Rh(D) and other red cell alloimmunization (Kell, Duffy), anti-D immune globulin prophylaxis, indirect Coombs titer monitoring, fetomaternal hemorrhage (Kleihauer-Betke), middle cerebral artery Doppler for fetal anemia
rh-alloimmunization.core: Maternal IgG against fetal red-cell antigens crosses the placenta, causing fetal anemia, hydrops, and neonatal hemolysis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Antigen-negative mother/positive fetus; prior pregnancy, transfusion, bleeding, trauma, invasive procedures
Anti-D, anti-Kell, and anti-Duffy clinically significant; ABO incompatibility usually milder

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic mother; fetal ascites, skin edema, placentomegaly, cardiomegaly
Neonate: early jaundice, pallor, reticulocytosis, **positive direct Coombs**; severe disease → cardiovascular collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
